title: Structure of arrays
description:
The obvious way to store particles is a vector of structs, each with a position and a velocity. But a loop that only reads positions then drags every velocity through the cache as well.

**Structure of arrays** turns it inside out: one tightly packed array per field. A loop that needs only `x` touches only the `x` array, and the processor reads memory in the straight line it is fastest at.

Write `class Particles` that stores four separate `std::vector<float>` (x, y, velocity x, velocity y):

- `std::size_t add(float x, float y, float vx, float vy)`: adds a particle and returns its index.
- `std::size_t size() const`
- `void step(float dt)`: moves every particle: `x += vx * dt`, `y += vy * dt`.
- `std::span<const float> xs() const` and `ys() const`: a view of each whole array.
- `float kineticEnergy() const`: the sum of `0.5 * (vx * vx + vy * vy)` over all particles.
- `void remove(std::size_t index)`: removes a particle with swap-and-pop on **all four** arrays, so they stay in step.
hints: `add` pushes one value onto each of the four vectors and returns the old size as the index.
Loops that update positions go over the indexes once: `m_x[i] += m_vx[i] * dt;` and the same for y.
